paragraphs.context: Last year, while my husband Will and I were doing research
paragraphs.mainIdea: A funny gorilla at the zoo.
paragraphs.simple: The writer and her husband visited a zoo in New York to learn about rain forests. A big gorilla looked at them hard and then pushed out her tongue at them, as if to make them laugh.

background.note: A very large zoo in the Bronx, a part of New York City.
Magic Tree House Research Guides are fact books that go with the stories.

paragraphs.context: We found out later that the gorilla’s name is Pattycake.
paragraphs.simple: The gorilla is called Pattycake. The writer keeps a photo of her on her desk. She feels that Pattycake is a big, kind friend who watches her work.

paragraphs.context: One summer day in Frog Creek, Pennsylvania, a mysterious tree house appeared
paragraphs.simple: One summer a strange tree house appeared in the woods near Jack and Annie's home in Frog Creek.

background.note: A state in the east of the United States.

paragraphs.context: Jack and Annie soon discovered that the tree house was magic.
paragraphs.simple: The tree house is magic. If they point to a picture in one of its books and make a wish, it takes them there. While they are away, time stops at home.

paragraphs.context: Along the way, Jack and Annie discovered that the tree house belongs to Morgan le Fay.
paragraphs.simple: The tree house belongs to Morgan le Fay, a magic librarian from King Arthur's Camelot. She travels through time to collect books.

background.note: In old stories about King Arthur, Morgan le Fay is a woman who can do magic. In these books she is a kind librarian.
The castle and city of King Arthur in old British stories.

paragraphs.context: In Magic Tree House Books #25–28, Jack and Annie learn about different kinds of magic.
paragraphs.simple: In earlier books they saved Morgan, saved old stories, saved a little dog and helped Camelot. Now, in books 25 to 28, they learn about different kinds of magic.

paragraphs.context: Jack sat up in bed. Rain tapped against his window.
paragraphs.simple: Jack wakes up at five in the morning. It is raining and still dark.

paragraphs.context: “Ready to find some special magic?” she asked.
paragraphs.simple: Annie asks if Jack is ready to look for a special magic. Jack wants to wait because it is dark and rainy.

paragraphs.context: “No waiting,” said Annie. “I’ll get an umbrella.
paragraphs.simple: Annie will bring an umbrella and Jack will bring a flashlight. They will meet downstairs.

paragraphs.context: Jack slipped downstairs and out the front door.
paragraphs.simple: Jack goes out quietly. Annie is waiting outside in jeans and a T-shirt. The air is cold and windy.

paragraphs.context: They headed through the Frog Creek woods.
paragraphs.simple: They walk through the woods. The flashlight shows wet leaves and branches, and then the rope ladder of the tree house.

paragraphs.context: “Yeah,” said Jack, smiling. “Theater magic.”
paragraphs.mainIdea: A memory of the last trip.
paragraphs.simple: The scrolls from their last trip, to old England, show that they found a special magic: the magic of the theater. Jack remembers acting in a play by Shakespeare.

background.note: William Shakespeare (1564 to 1616) was an English writer of plays and poems. In book 25, Jack and Annie acted in one of his plays.

paragraphs.context: He shined the flashlight on a book lying under the window.
paragraphs.simple: Jack sees a book under the window. A piece of paper is sticking out of it. It is a note from Morgan.

paragraphs.context: Good luck on your second journey to find a special magic.
paragraphs.simple: Morgan wishes them good luck on their second trip to find a special magic. A secret rhyme will help them.

paragraphs.context: Jack shined the flashlight on the cover of the book.
paragraphs.simple: The cover of the book shows huge trees in mist. The title is "An African Rain Forest".

paragraphs.context: “Rain forest?” said Jack. “Good thing we brought our umbrella and flashlight.
paragraphs.simple: Jack is glad they brought an umbrella and a flashlight. He remembers how dark and rainy the Amazon rain forest was.

background.note: The Amazon is a very big river and rain forest in South America. Jack and Annie went there in book 6.

paragraphs.context: “Well … ,” said Jack, “not all rain forests have big rivers.
paragraphs.simple: Annie remembers spiders, snakes and crocodiles. Jack says that not all rain forests are the same.

paragraphs.context: But it was too late. The wind was blowing harder.
paragraphs.simple: Before Jack can stop her, Annie makes the wish. The wind blows and the tree house spins.

paragraphs.context: The misty rain forest in the mountains of central Africa is called a “cloud forest.”
paragraphs.simple: The book says that the misty rain forest in the mountains of central Africa is called a cloud forest.

background.note: The middle part of Africa, around countries like Rwanda, Uganda and the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

paragraphs.context: The African cloud forest is home to many animals
paragraphs.simple: The book lists animals that live there: elephants, water buffaloes and black leopards. Jack stops when he reads "black leopards".

paragraphs.context: “I don’t know about that,” said Jack. He pictured huge apes pounding their chests.
paragraphs.simple: Jack thinks of big apes beating their chests. He wants to study gorillas and write notes about what they do, like a real scientist.

paragraphs.context: Jack threw his notebook, the research book, and the flashlight into his pack.
paragraphs.simple: Jack puts his things in his backpack, hangs the umbrella on his arm and goes down the ladder after Annie.

paragraphs.context: Jack and Annie started through the cloud forest.
paragraphs.simple: They walk around huge trees covered with moss and push past tall bushes and plants.

paragraphs.context: She pointed to a fat tree. It had wide lower limbs padded with thick cushions of moss.
paragraphs.simple: Annie shows Jack a fat tree. Its low branches are covered in thick, soft moss. It looks like a big armchair.

paragraphs.context: He put the umbrella on the ground.
paragraphs.simple: Jack puts the umbrella and the flashlight on the ground next to the tree and starts to draw it.

paragraphs.context: “Maybe we should go back up to the tree house,” he said.
paragraphs.simple: Jack hears branches break. He thinks it might be a leopard and wants to go back to the tree house to read more.

paragraphs.context: The gorilla’s fur was very black against the green leaves.
paragraphs.simple: The gorilla has black fur, large nostrils, small ears and bright brown eyes. She looks like she wants to play.

paragraphs.context: The gorilla hid behind the leaves again. Then she poked her head out.
paragraphs.simple: The gorilla hides and then shows her face. Annie says "Peekaboo!" The gorilla claps and pushes out her tongue.

paragraphs.context: Jack rolled his eyes. “Don’t name her Bu-bu,” he said to Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Annie calls the gorilla Bu-bu. Jack thinks Annie always wants every animal to be her best friend.

paragraphs.context: Carrying his notebook, Jack hurried in the direction of the noise.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie and the gorilla in the trees.
paragraphs.simple: Jack runs toward the noise. Annie and the gorilla are sitting up in two trees, playing.

paragraphs.context: He noticed she was about the size of a three-year-old kid.
paragraphs.simple: Jack sees that the gorilla is as big as a three-year-old child. Her fingers look like human fingers, with nails.

paragraphs.context: Jack looked around. Light was fading quickly from the forest.
paragraphs.simple: The light is going fast. Jack is not sure if night is coming or a storm.

paragraphs.context: Annie threw down her bark. She grabbed a tree branch and tried to swing to another tree.
paragraphs.simple: Annie does everything the gorilla does. When the gorilla swings to another tree, Annie tries too.

paragraphs.context: Annie didn’t swing like a gorilla. She fell from the tree
paragraphs.simple: Annie cannot swing like a gorilla. She falls and hits the ground near Jack.

paragraphs.context: The gorilla bounded down the tree and over to Annie.
paragraphs.simple: The gorilla jumps down to Annie. She bites her lip, as if she is worried.

paragraphs.context: “Yes—” Annie panted, “just—got the breath—knocked out of me—”
paragraphs.simple: Annie can hardly speak because the fall pushed all the air out of her body. But she can move her arms and legs, so nothing is broken.

paragraphs.context: He took off his jacket and draped it over her.
paragraphs.simple: Jack puts his jacket over Annie to keep her dry. He tells the gorilla to stay with her and goes back for the umbrella and flashlight.

paragraphs.context: As he peered through the growing darkness, Jack saw many fat trees.
paragraphs.mainIdea: All the trees look the same.
paragraphs.simple: It is getting dark. Jack sees many fat trees with moss, and he cannot find the right one.

paragraphs.context: Forget the umbrella and flashlight, he thought.
paragraphs.simple: Jack decides to forget the umbrella and flashlight. It is more important to get back to Annie before it is too dark.

paragraphs.context: Jack put out his hands. He moved slowly through the dark, rainy forest.
paragraphs.simple: Jack moves slowly with his hands in front of him. He calls for Annie and Bu-bu, but he cannot hear anything except the rain.

paragraphs.context: As he jumped back, he slipped and fell in the mud.
paragraphs.simple: Jack falls in the mud. He sits between two big roots of a tree and decides to wait there until morning.

paragraphs.context: As rain dripped all around him, Jack wondered if leopards came out at night.
paragraphs.simple: Jack wonders if leopards come out at night. He tries not to think about it and thinks about going home.

paragraphs.context: “To find a special magic … ,” he whispered.
paragraphs.simple: Jack tries to say Morgan's rhyme, but he cannot remember the rest. He feels tired and very unhappy, and he closes his eyes.

paragraphs.context: Jack stood up. His arms and legs felt stiff and achy.
paragraphs.simple: After the night on the ground, Jack's body hurts and his wet clothes stick to him.

paragraphs.context: As the small gorilla led him through the cloud forest
paragraphs.simple: Bu-bu takes Jack through the forest. She stops in front of a row of bushes.

paragraphs.context: Large dark figures were sleeping in an open, grassy area—gorillas!
paragraphs.simple: Jack sees at least ten gorillas sleeping in an open, grassy place.

paragraphs.context: The gorillas were all sizes.
paragraphs.simple: The smallest gorilla is a baby in its mother's arms. The biggest is a giant with black and silver fur.

paragraphs.context: Mountain gorillas live together in families.
paragraphs.simple: The book says: gorillas live in families. A big male with silver fur on his back leads the family. Gorillas do not hunt animals; they eat plants. They are shy and gentle.

paragraphs.context: Jack didn’t know what to do. If he called her name, the gorillas would wake up.
paragraphs.simple: Annie is asleep on the other side of the gorillas. Jack cannot call her, so he must go over to her quietly.

paragraphs.context: As he started toward Annie, he heard a grunt.
paragraphs.simple: The giant gorilla with silver fur opens his eyes and sits up when he sees Jack.

paragraphs.context: Jack’s stick made the gorilla growl.
paragraphs.simple: Jack picks up a stick, but it makes the gorilla angry. The gorilla stands up. He is very big.

paragraphs.context: The silverback growled again. His long, shaggy arms touched the ground.
paragraphs.simple: The silverback walks toward Jack on his knuckles. Jack steps back again and again.

paragraphs.context: Before Jack could say “peace,” the giant gorilla went crazy.
paragraphs.simple: Jack starts to say "I come in peace", but the gorilla hoots, jumps up, shakes a tree, tears leaves and beats his chest.

paragraphs.context: The gorilla dropped on all fours. He charged back and forth past Jack.
paragraphs.simple: The gorilla runs back and forth past Jack, then throws himself on the ground and hits it with his hands.

paragraphs.context: Jack opened his eyes. He peeked around the tree.
paragraphs.simple: The noise stops. The silverback sits on the ground and smiles. He looks happy with himself.

paragraphs.context: Jack didn’t know whether to be scared or to laugh.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack still has to reach Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Jack does not know if he should be afraid or laugh. He knows that he must still get to Annie.

paragraphs.context: To safely get close to gorillas in the wild, it’s wise to act like a gorilla yourself.
paragraphs.mainIdea: How to be safe near gorillas.
paragraphs.simple: The book says: to be safe near wild gorillas, act like a gorilla. Go down low on your knuckles, keep your head down and be friendly.

paragraphs.context: Jack took a deep breath. He smiled a friendly smile.
paragraphs.simple: Jack goes down on his knuckles, smiles and moves out from behind the tree. It hurts his fingers.

paragraphs.context: When he got to the edge of the clearing, he glanced back.
paragraphs.simple: The giant gorilla follows Jack. He is frowning, but he does not attack.

paragraphs.context: More gorillas were waking up. A large gorilla hugged Bu-bu as if to comfort her.
paragraphs.simple: Other gorillas wake up. When Bu-bu sees Jack she cries out happily, and all the gorillas look at him.

paragraphs.context: “No!” she said. “When you didn’t come back, Bu-bu led me here.
paragraphs.simple: When Jack did not come back, Bu-bu took Annie to the gorillas. It was too dark for Annie to see them.

paragraphs.context: Another small gorilla left his mother and ran over to Annie, too.
paragraphs.simple: Another young gorilla, about as big as a two-year-old child, comes to play with Annie. She calls him Ho-ho.

paragraphs.context: Jack felt a little jealous. He wanted the gorillas to like him as well.
paragraphs.simple: Jack wishes the gorillas liked him too. He does not know how to join the fun, so he writes notes instead.

paragraphs.context: “That big guy doesn’t understand what you’re doing!”
paragraphs.simple: Annie tells Jack that the silverback does not understand what he is doing. Jack puts his notebook away.

paragraphs.context: The gorillas began lining up behind the silverback.
paragraphs.simple: The gorillas walk in a line behind the silverback. Babies ride with their mothers. Bu-bu holds Annie's hand.

paragraphs.context: Jack smiled shyly. He took Bu-bu’s small, warm hand.
paragraphs.simple: Bu-bu holds out her hand to Jack. He takes it and walks with the gorillas.

paragraphs.context: On their ramble through the cloud forest, the gorillas found food everywhere.
paragraphs.simple: The gorillas eat flowers, ferns, leaves, small branches and tree bark as they walk. They swallow and make burping sounds.

paragraphs.context: Annie didn’t seem to mind, either.
paragraphs.simple: It rains again, but nobody cares. Annie and Bu-bu run around the trees, laughing and crying out.

paragraphs.context: Jack quickly tried to act like a gorilla.
paragraphs.simple: When the silverback frowns at him, Jack acts like a gorilla. He bites a leaf, but it tastes very bad, so he only pretends to eat it.

paragraphs.context: Jack felt a tap on his back. He jumped. But it was just Ho-ho.
paragraphs.simple: Ho-ho gives Jack a small branch to eat. Jack politely takes it and says he will eat it later.

paragraphs.context: Jack munched the berries. To his surprise, they tasted good.
paragraphs.simple: The berries from Ho-ho's mother taste good. Jack burps like a gorilla, and this time he is not pretending.

paragraphs.context: Actually, he was having fun now.
paragraphs.simple: Jack is having fun. He does not mind the rain, and he feels that the gorillas really like him.

paragraphs.context: Big Guy led his family into a clearing.
paragraphs.simple: After eating, the silverback, now called Big Guy, takes his family to a sunny clearing.

paragraphs.context: Ho-ho’s mom made a bed of weed stalks for Ho-ho.
paragraphs.simple: The mothers make beds of plants for their children. Bu-bu's mother makes beds for Jack and Annie too.

paragraphs.context: Lying on his leafy bed, Jack watched the mother of the baby gorilla groom her small baby.
paragraphs.simple: Jack watches a mother gorilla look through her baby's hair and clean his skin.

paragraphs.context: The baby soon wiggled free and crawled around in the grass.
paragraphs.simple: The mother gorilla starts to look through Annie's hair. Jack thinks she is looking for bugs.

paragraphs.context: “Hi, Little Guy,” Annie said tenderly.
paragraphs.simple: Annie picks up the baby gorilla, calls him Little Guy and gently touches his head.

paragraphs.simple: The book says that gorillas are very clever. A gorilla named Koko, who lives with people, has learned sign language.

background.note: A real gorilla (1971 to 2018) who lived in California and learned to use many hand signs.

paragraphs.context: “Morgan’s secret rhyme!” said Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Annie remembers Morgan's rhyme: "speak a special language". Sign language is a special language!

paragraphs.context: “I even know a little sign language,” said Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Annie learned how to sign "I love you" at school.

paragraphs.context: Annie held up a closed hand. Slowly she lifted her thumb, index finger, and little finger.
paragraphs.simple: To make the sign, Annie closes her hand, then puts up her thumb, her first finger and her little finger.

paragraphs.context: The two little gorillas stared at Annie and Jack.
paragraphs.simple: Bu-bu and Ho-ho try to make the same sign with their hands. Annie thinks they love them too.

paragraphs.context: Ho-ho held his little arms above his head.
paragraphs.simple: Ho-ho jumps at Jack and knocks him over. The young gorillas want to play.

paragraphs.context: Bu-bu jumped on Jack and put him in a headlock.
paragraphs.simple: Jack gets away from the gorillas and runs into the forest. Bu-bu and Ho-ho run after him.

paragraphs.context: Bu-bu screeched and leaped straight up in the air.
paragraphs.simple: Jack jumps out and shouts "BOO!" Bu-bu jumps with fright. Jack laughs, but Bu-bu hides her face.

paragraphs.context: Bu-bu wrapped her arms around Annie’s neck.
paragraphs.simple: Bu-bu holds on to Annie and hides her head on Annie's shoulder. Annie tells her that Jack was only playing.

paragraphs.context: Bu-bu stuck her tongue out at him.
paragraphs.simple: Bu-bu pushes out her tongue at Jack and then smiles a big smile. They are friends again.

paragraphs.context: Just then, Ho-ho started screeching.
paragraphs.simple: Ho-ho is crying out and pointing at the bushes. Little Guy is not there.

paragraphs.context: A huge, sleek cat with black fur was sitting on the branch.
paragraphs.simple: A big black leopard is sitting on a branch above the baby. Its light green eyes look hungry.

paragraphs.context: The leopard let out a snarl.
paragraphs.simple: Annie picks up the baby. The leopard makes an angry sound and moves slowly toward them.

paragraphs.context: Jack panicked. He didn’t know what to do at first.
paragraphs.simple: Jack is very afraid. Then he remembers Big Guy's show. He takes a deep breath and hoots loudly.

paragraphs.context: Jack grabbed a tree limb and shook it.
paragraphs.simple: Jack does what Big Guy did: he shakes a branch, pulls off leaves and beats his chest.

paragraphs.context: “He’s gone,” Annie said in a quiet voice.
paragraphs.simple: Annie tells Jack that the leopard went away some time ago. Jack sits up and smiles.

paragraphs.context: Jack couldn’t stop smiling. He had scared off a leopard!
paragraphs.simple: Jack is very happy because he made the leopard go away. The gorillas and Annie look at him with wonder.

paragraphs.context: The giant gorilla walked silently over to Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Big Guy takes the baby from Annie and gently touches her face.

paragraphs.context: But the silverback patted him on the head.
paragraphs.simple: Jack thinks Big Guy will hit him, but the gorilla gently touches his head. Jack feels warm and happy.

paragraphs.context: “Yeah,” said Annie. “He must have watched the show you put on.
paragraphs.simple: Annie thinks Big Guy saw Jack's show and was proud of him. Jack says Big Guy was proud of Annie too.

paragraphs.context: “Good-bye?” said Jack. He didn’t want to say good-bye to the gorillas.
paragraphs.simple: Annie says they must go now. Jack does not want to say good-bye. He loves the gorillas.

paragraphs.context: They found all the gorillas awake.
paragraphs.simple: In the clearing, the gorillas are awake. Some stretch and open their mouths wide; others eat grass or leaves.

paragraphs.context: “Thanks for letting us be a part of your family,” said Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Annie thanks the gorillas for letting them be part of their family. The gorillas look sad.

paragraphs.context: Big Guy lifted his hand in the air as if he were about to wave.
paragraphs.simple: Big Guy does not wave. He makes the sign for "I love you" with his hand.

paragraphs.context: The silverback stared at them for a long moment with a gentle, shy look.
paragraphs.simple: Big Guy looks at them kindly for a long time. Then he calls his family, and they walk away behind him.

paragraphs.context: Jack couldn’t talk. His heart was too full.
paragraphs.simple: Jack is too sad to speak. He starts to walk after the gorillas, but Annie says he is going the wrong way.

paragraphs.context: “And don’t forget these,” said Annie.
paragraphs.simple: On the way back, Annie picks up Jack's backpack, his jacket, and then the umbrella and flashlight under the fat tree.

paragraphs.context: Suddenly, a joyous screech rang out.
paragraphs.simple: Just before they go home, they hear a happy gorilla cry. The sound goes straight to Jack's heart.

paragraphs.context: “I miss them already,” he said.
paragraphs.simple: They are home, and Jack already misses the gorillas.

paragraphs.context: “I listed a few things about them,” he said.
paragraphs.simple: Jack says that lists do not tell you much. You must love gorillas to really know them.

paragraphs.context: “I promised Ho-ho I’d eat this later,” he said.
paragraphs.simple: Jack keeps Ho-ho's small branch for Morgan. It will show her that they found a special magic: the magic of all animals.

paragraphs.context: Jack didn’t mind, though.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack does not care about the rain.
paragraphs.simple: It is still cold, dark and rainy, but Jack does not put on his jacket or use the flashlight or the umbrella.

paragraphs.context: Jack felt as if he weren’t completely human yet.
paragraphs.simple: Jack feels that a little bit of gorilla is still in him. He and Annie make gorilla sounds together.

paragraphs.context: Gorillas are the biggest members of the group of animals we call primates.
paragraphs.simple: Gorillas are the biggest primates. Primates are a group of animals that includes chimpanzees, monkeys and people.

paragraphs.context: All gorillas live in Africa.
paragraphs.simple: All gorillas live in Africa. There are western lowland, eastern lowland and mountain gorillas. Mountain gorillas are the biggest.

paragraphs.context: Mountain gorillas live in the volcanic mountains of Virunga in east-central Africa.
paragraphs.simple: Mountain gorillas live in the Virunga mountains, which were made by volcanoes. The name means "a lonely mountain that reaches to the clouds".

background.note: A line of volcano mountains in east-central Africa, on the borders of Rwanda, Uganda and the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

paragraphs.context: All gorillas are on the endangered species list.
paragraphs.simple: All gorillas could die out, but mountain gorillas are in the most danger. Fewer than 650 live in the wild. Dian Fossey lived with them for almost 20 years and worked hard to protect them.

paragraphs.context: Since 1971, a lowland gorilla named Koko has been part of
paragraphs.simple: Gorillas cannot speak like people. But a woman taught a gorilla named Koko to use sign language, which uses the hands. Koko knows more than 1,000 signs and about 2,000 English words.

sentences.context: Last year, while my husband Will and I were doing research for our Magic Tree House Research Guide on rain forests, we visited the Bronx Zoo in New York.
sentences.simple: Last year my husband and I went to a zoo in New York. We wanted to learn about rain forests for one of our fact books.
sentences.main: We visited the Bronx Zoo.

parts.meaning: A year ago,

parts.text: while my husband Will and I were doing research for our Magic Tree House Research Guide on rain forests,
parts.job: What they were doing at that time.
parts.meaning: when my husband Will and I were finding facts about rain forests for our fact book,

parts.text: we visited the Bronx Zoo in New York.
parts.meaning: we went to the Bronx Zoo in New York.

sentences.grammar: "While" + past continuous ("were doing") gives a longer action; the main part ("we visited") is a shorter action at that time.

sentences.context: And I hope that by the time you finish reading Good Morning, Gorillas, you’ll love them as much as I do.
sentences.simple: I hope that when you finish this book, you will love gorillas as much as I do.
sentences.main: I hope that you’ll love them.

parts.meaning: And I wish

parts.text: that by the time you finish reading Good Morning, Gorillas,
parts.meaning: that when you finish reading this book,

parts.text: you’ll love them as much as I do.
parts.meaning: you will love gorillas as much as I love them.

sentences.grammar: "By the time" + present tense talks about the future. "As much as I do" compares two things: your love and my love.

sentences.context: All they had to do was point to a picture and wish to go there.
sentences.simple: They only needed to point to a picture and wish to go to that place.
sentences.main: All they had to do was point and wish.

parts.meaning: The only thing they needed to do
was to point to a picture
and wish to go to that place.

sentences.grammar: "All you have to do is ..." means it is very easy: you only need to do this. After "All ... do was", the verb has no "to": "was point".

sentences.context: He had great memories of acting in a play by their friend William Shakespeare.
sentences.simple: He remembered happily how he acted in a play by their friend Shakespeare.
sentences.main: He had great memories.

parts.meaning: He remembered good things
about acting in a play
written by their friend William Shakespeare.

sentences.grammar: After "of", use the -ing form: "memories of acting".

sentences.context: It showed huge trees partly hidden by mist.
sentences.simple: The picture showed very big trees. Mist covered some parts of them.
sentences.main: It showed huge trees.

parts.meaning: The cover had a picture of very big trees
that mist was covering a little.

sentences.grammar: "Hidden by mist" is a past participle group. It tells you more about the trees, like "which were partly hidden by mist".

sentences.context: The misty rain forest in the mountains of central Africa is called a “cloud forest.”
sentences.simple: People call the misty rain forest in the mountains of central Africa a "cloud forest".
sentences.main: The misty rain forest is called a “cloud forest.”

parts.meaning: The rain forest full of mist

parts.text: in the mountains of central Africa
parts.meaning: high in the mountains in the middle of Africa
has the name "cloud forest".

sentences.grammar: "Is called" (passive) gives the name of something.

sentences.context: Write down their habits and behavior, just like a real scientist.
sentences.simple: I would write down what they usually do and how they act, the way a real scientist does.
sentences.main: Write down their habits and behavior.

parts.text: Write down their habits and behavior,
parts.meaning: Write notes about what gorillas usually do and how they act,
in the same way as a real scientist.

sentences.grammar: This sentence has no subject. Jack is still talking about what he would like to do: "(I'd like to) write down ...".

sentences.context: It had wide lower limbs padded with thick cushions of moss.
sentences.simple: Its low branches were wide, and thick, soft moss covered them like cushions.
sentences.main: It had wide lower limbs.

parts.meaning: The tree had wide low branches

parts.text: padded with thick cushions of moss.
parts.meaning: covered with thick, soft moss, like cushions.

sentences.grammar: "Padded with ..." is a past participle group that tells you more about the limbs.

sentences.context: She was grinning from ear to ear as she stared into the bushes.
sentences.simple: She smiled a very big smile while she looked into the bushes.
sentences.main: She was grinning from ear to ear.

parts.text: She was grinning from ear to ear
parts.meaning: She was smiling very widely

parts.text: as she stared into the bushes.
parts.meaning: while she looked hard into the bushes.

sentences.grammar: "As" here means "while": two things happen at the same time.

sentences.context: Her bright brown eyes were full of mischief.
sentences.simple: Her bright brown eyes showed that she wanted to play tricks.
sentences.main: Her eyes were full of mischief.

parts.meaning: Her shiny brown eyes
looked naughty and ready to play.

sentences.grammar: "Full of" + a noun means having a lot of it.

sentences.context: To his relief, the gorilla settled on a branch.
sentences.simple: Jack was glad when the gorilla sat down on a branch and stopped climbing.
sentences.main: The gorilla settled on a branch.

parts.meaning: Jack was glad that

parts.text: the gorilla settled on a branch.
parts.meaning: the gorilla sat down and stayed on a branch.

sentences.grammar: "To his relief" / "to my surprise" at the start of a sentence tells you how someone felt about what happened.

sentences.context: She bit her lower lip as if she were worried.
sentences.simple: She bit her lip. She looked worried.
sentences.main: She bit her lip.

parts.meaning: She pressed her teeth on her bottom lip
like someone who is worried.

sentences.grammar: After "as if", the book uses "were" (not "was") for something that only seems true.

sentences.context: He realized that both a storm and night had come to the forest.
sentences.simple: He understood that a storm had started and night had come.
sentences.main: He realized something.

parts.meaning: He suddenly understood

parts.text: that both a storm and night had come to the forest.
parts.meaning: that a storm and the night had both arrived in the forest.

sentences.grammar: "Both ... and ..." joins two things. "Had come" (past perfect) happened before he realized it.

sentences.context: It was more important to get back to Annie before it was too dark.
sentences.simple: Getting back to Annie before it got too dark was more important.
sentences.main: It was more important to get back to Annie.

parts.meaning: It mattered more
to return to Annie
before there was no light at all.

sentences.grammar: "It was + adjective + to + verb": "it" stands for the "to" part.

sentences.context: But he couldn’t hear anything above the loud patter of the rain.
sentences.simple: He could not hear anything because the rain was too loud.
sentences.main: He couldn’t hear anything.

parts.meaning: But he heard nothing

parts.text: above the loud patter of the rain.
parts.meaning: because the noise of the rain was louder.

sentences.grammar: "Above" a noise means louder than it, so you cannot hear past it.

sentences.context: Their fun adventure in the cloud forest had turned into a nightmare.
sentences.simple: Their happy trip in the cloud forest had become very bad and scary.
sentences.main: Their adventure had turned into a nightmare.

parts.text: Their fun adventure in the cloud forest
parts.meaning: Their exciting trip in the cloud forest
had become a very bad dream.

sentences.grammar: "Turn into" means change and become. "Had turned" (past perfect) shows it happened before this moment.

sentences.context: The leader of the family is a large male called a “silverback” because he has silver fur on his back and shoulders.
sentences.simple: A big male gorilla leads the family. He is called a silverback because the fur on his back is silver.
sentences.main: The leader is a large male.

parts.meaning: The gorilla who leads the family
is a big male
with the name "silverback"

parts.text: because he has silver fur on his back and shoulders.
parts.meaning: because the hair on his back and shoulders is silver.

sentences.grammar: "Called ..." gives a name. "Because" gives the reason for the name.

sentences.context: If he called her name, the gorillas would wake up.
sentences.simple: If he shouted her name, the noise would wake the gorillas.
sentences.main: The gorillas would wake up.

parts.meaning: If he shouted "Annie!",
the gorillas would stop sleeping.

sentences.grammar: "If" + past tense, then "would" + verb: this talks about something that is not happening but could.

sentences.context: He waited for the maniac gorilla to find him and tear him to pieces.
sentences.simple: He waited, sure that the wild gorilla would find him and hurt him badly.
sentences.main: He waited.

parts.meaning: He stayed and waited

parts.text: for the maniac gorilla to find him
parts.meaning: for the crazy gorilla to find him
and pull him apart.

sentences.grammar: "Wait for someone to do something": the person comes after "for", then "to" + verb.

sentences.context: To safely get close to gorillas in the wild, it’s wise to act like a gorilla yourself.
sentences.simple: If you want to go near wild gorillas safely, it is a good idea to act like a gorilla.
sentences.main: It’s wise to act like a gorilla yourself.

parts.text: To safely get close to gorillas in the wild,
parts.meaning: If you want to go near wild gorillas without danger,

parts.text: it’s wise to act like a gorilla yourself.
parts.meaning: it is a good idea to act like a gorilla.

sentences.grammar: The first "to" part gives the purpose. "Yourself" makes "you" stronger: you, too, act like one.

sentences.context: He was frowning, but he didn’t seem about to attack.
sentences.simple: He looked unhappy, but he did not look ready to fight.
sentences.main: He was frowning.

parts.meaning: He had an unhappy face,

parts.text: but he didn’t seem about to attack.
parts.meaning: but it did not look as if he would attack soon.

sentences.grammar: "About to" + verb means going to do it very soon.

sentences.context: Some of the gorillas really seemed to like him, he thought.
sentences.simple: Jack thought that some of the gorillas really liked him.
sentences.main: Some of the gorillas seemed to like him.

parts.text: Some of the gorillas really seemed to like him,
parts.meaning: Some gorillas looked as if they really liked him,
Jack thought.

sentences.grammar: "He thought" at the end shows these are Jack's thoughts. "Seem to" + verb means it looks true.

sentences.context: Sign language is a special language used by people who cannot hear.
sentences.simple: Sign language is a language of hand movements. People who cannot hear use it.
sentences.main: Sign language is a special language.

parts.text: Sign language is a special language
parts.meaning: Sign language is a special way to talk
that people use
who are not able to hear.

sentences.grammar: "Used by ..." (past participle) tells you more about the language. "Who" tells you more about the people.

sentences.context: Jack felt as if the top of his head were glowing.
sentences.simple: Jack felt so happy that the top of his head seemed to shine.
sentences.main: Jack felt as if his head were glowing.

parts.meaning: Jack had the feeling

parts.text: as if the top of his head were glowing.
parts.meaning: that the top of his head was shining with warmth.

sentences.grammar: "As if" + "were" describes something that is not really true but feels true.

sentences.context: Big Guy lifted his hand in the air as if he were about to wave.
sentences.simple: Big Guy put his hand up. It looked as if he was going to wave.
sentences.main: Big Guy lifted his hand.

parts.text: Big Guy lifted his hand in the air
parts.meaning: Big Guy put his hand up

parts.text: as if he were about to wave.
parts.meaning: like someone who is going to wave good-bye.

sentences.grammar: "As if he were about to ..." means it looked like he was going to do it very soon.

sentences.context: The happy, wild sound shot through the white mist, through the cool rain, straight into Jack’s heart.
sentences.simple: The happy, wild cry went quickly through the mist and the rain, right into Jack's heart.
sentences.main: The sound shot into Jack’s heart.

parts.meaning: The happy, wild cry
went fast through the white mist,
through the cool rain,
right into Jack's heart.

sentences.grammar: The writer repeats "through ..." to make the sentence move, like the sound moving.

sentences.context: You have to love gorillas to really know them.
sentences.simple: If you want to really know gorillas, you must love them.
sentences.main: You have to love gorillas.

parts.meaning: You must love gorillas
if you want to understand them well.

sentences.grammar: "Have to" means must. "To" + verb at the end gives the purpose.

sentences.context: They keep on the move, so they will not deplete a feeding area.
sentences.simple: They keep moving to new places, so they do not eat all the plants in one place.
sentences.main: They keep on the move.

parts.meaning: They go on moving from place to place,

parts.text: so they will not deplete a feeding area.
parts.meaning: so that they do not use up all the food in one place.

sentences.grammar: "So" here means "so that": it gives the reason for the first part.

a bit of.example: There was still a bit of gorilla left in him.

all my best.meaning: A friendly way to end a letter, like "Best wishes".

along the way.meaning: While doing something; during a trip or a time.
along the way.example: Along the way, Jack and Annie discovered that the tree house belongs to Morgan le Fay.

as if.meaning: In a way that makes it seem that something is true.
as if.example: I feel as if she’s a giant, friendly spirit

as soon as.example: As soon as he was gone, Jack spat out the leaf.

at first.meaning: At the start, before something changes.
at first.example: He didn’t know what to do at first.

at least.meaning: Not less than. "At least ten" means ten or more.
at least.example: There were at least ten of them.

back and forth.meaning: First one way and then the other way, again and again.
back and forth.example: He charged back and forth past Jack.

be about to.meaning: To be going to do something very soon.
be about to.example: he didn’t seem about to attack.

break free.meaning: To get away from someone who is holding you.
break free.example: Jack broke free from the two small gorillas.

break off.meaning: To take a piece from something by breaking it.
break off.example: The gorilla broke off a piece of tree bark.

can't believe one's eyes.meaning: To be very surprised by what you see.

candy bar.meaning: A long, thin piece of sweet food, often chocolate. (British English: chocolate bar.)
candy bar.example: She nibbled it like a candy bar.

catch a glimpse.meaning: To see something for a very short time.
catch a glimpse.example: Jack hoped to catch one last glimpse of the gorilla family.

catch one's breath.meaning: 1. To stop breathing for a moment because you are afraid or surprised. 2. To rest until you can breathe normally again.

catch up with.meaning: To reach someone who is ahead of you.
catch up with.example: He moved around the tree and caught up with Annie.

chatter away.meaning: To talk and talk quickly about small things.
chatter away.example: Bu-bu and Ho-ho were chattering away to their moms.

clear one's throat.meaning: To make a small sound in your throat before you speak.
clear one's throat.example: Jack cleared his throat and kept reading:

close by.example: The silverback was standing close by.

cloud forest.meaning: A rain forest high in the mountains, where clouds and mist are always around the trees.
cloud forest.example: The African cloud forest is home to many animals

come along.example: I don’t think they want me to come along

come out.meaning: To go outside, or come out of a place where you were hidden.
come out.example: Jack wondered if leopards came out at night.

come to a stop.example: Slowly the feeding came to a stop.

crack up.meaning: (Friendly talk.) To start laughing a lot.

cross one's face.meaning: "A smile crossed her face" means a smile came onto her face.
cross one's face.example: A joyful smile crossed her face.

far apart.meaning: A long way from each other.

fast asleep.example: Annie was fast asleep in the grass!

find out.meaning: To learn something that you did not know.
find out.example: We found out later that the gorilla’s name is Pattycake.

from ear to ear.meaning: "Grinning from ear to ear" means smiling a very big smile.
from ear to ear.example: She was grinning from ear to ear

get close to.example: To safely get close to gorillas in the wild

get it.meaning: (Friendly talk.) To understand. "I get it" means "I understand."

give up.meaning: To stop trying to do something.
give up.example: Jack tried to follow them, but he gave up.

go crazy.meaning: To start acting in a wild, crazy way.

go on.meaning: To happen. "What's going on?" means "What is happening?"

good luck.meaning: Words you say when you hope that things go well for someone.
good luck.example: Good luck on your second journey to find a special magic.

good thing.meaning: "Good thing we brought ..." means it is lucky that we brought it.
good thing.example: Good thing we brought our umbrella and flashlight.

hold out.meaning: To move your hand toward someone, often to give them something.
hold out.example: She held out her free hand to him.

in a panic.meaning: Very afraid and not able to think clearly.
in a panic.example: Jack crouched down in a panic.

in fact.meaning: Really; and more than that. You use it to add something true and surprising.
in fact.example: In fact, we still laugh whenever we think about that moment.

in the wild.meaning: In nature, not in a zoo.
in the wild.example: To safely get close to gorillas in the wild

index finger.meaning: The finger next to your thumb.
index finger.example: Slowly she lifted her thumb, index finger, and little finger.

join in.meaning: To start doing something together with other people.
join in.example: But he didn’t know how to join in the fun.

just in case.example: He picked it up—just in case.

just then.example: Just then, he felt a drop of water hit his arm.

keep dry.meaning: To stay dry; not get wet.
keep dry.example: he stood under a mossy tree to keep dry.

knock over.meaning: To hit someone or something so that they fall down.
knock over.example: With a flying tackle, he knocked Jack over.

lead the way.meaning: To go first, so others can follow you.
lead the way.example: She led the way back through the shrubs

leap to one's feet.example: He hooted and leaped to his feet.

left out.meaning: Not part of a group; not asked to join in.
left out.example: He didn’t feel so left out.

let out.meaning: To make a sound; or to breathe out.
let out.example: The leopard let out a snarl.

lie down.meaning: To put your body flat, for example on a bed. (Past tense: lay down.)
lie down.example: The silverback lay down and tucked his arms under his head.

light up.meaning: To give light to something so that you can see it.
light up.example: The flashlight lit up the trees

line up.meaning: To stand in a line, one behind the other.
line up.example: The gorillas began lining up behind the silverback.

look for.example: “She’s looking for bugs, I think,” said Jack.

make a list.meaning: To write things down one under the other.
make a list.example: Then he made a list in his notebook.

now and then.example: picking at his skin now and then.

on all fours.meaning: On your hands and knees, or on hands and feet, like an animal.
on all fours.example: The gorilla dropped on all fours.

on one's hands and knees.meaning: With your hands and knees on the ground.
on one's hands and knees.example: Jack scrambled on his hands and knees over to a tree.

out of sight.meaning: Too far away to be seen.
out of sight.example: Then he and the small gorillas moved out of sight.

pack up.meaning: To put things away in a bag.
pack up.example: Jack packed up his research book.

pick up.meaning: To lift something up with your hand.
pick up.example: He picked it up—just in case.

play tag.meaning: To play a game where one child runs after the others and tries to touch one.
play tag.example: She and Bu-bu played tag in the drizzly woods.

pleased with oneself.meaning: Happy and proud about something you did.

proud of.meaning: Happy about something good that another person did.

pull on.meaning: To put on clothes or a bag quickly.

pull out.meaning: To take something out of a bag or a pocket.
pull out.example: He pulled out his notebook and wrote:

push away.meaning: To try not to think about something.
push away.example: He quickly pushed the thought away.

put away.meaning: To put something back in its place, or in a bag.
put away.example: He quickly put away his notebook.

put on.meaning: 1. To dress yourself in clothes. 2. To "put on a show" is to do something so that other people watch.
put on.example: He pulled on his clothes and put on a jacket.

put out.meaning: To hold out your hand or arm in front of you.

put up.meaning: To open an umbrella and hold it up.
put up.example: He didn’t put up the umbrella.

rain forest.meaning: A thick forest in a hot, wet place, where it rains a lot.
rain forest.example: doing research for our Magic Tree House Research Guide on rain forests

reach for.meaning: To move your hand or arm toward something to take it.
reach for.example: Just then, the baby’s mother reached for him.

read aloud.meaning: To read words in a voice that other people can hear.
read aloud.example: Jack shined his light on the paper while Annie read aloud:

ring out.meaning: For a sound: to be heard loudly and clearly.
ring out.example: Suddenly, a joyous screech rang out.

roll one's eyes.meaning: To move your eyes up and around, to show that you think something is silly.

rope ladder.meaning: A ladder made of rope, which hangs down.
rope ladder.example: Then it shined on a dangling rope ladder.

run into.meaning: To hit something by accident while you are moving.
run into.example: He had run into something that felt like a ball of spiderwebs!

say good-bye.example: “We have to say good-bye now,” said Annie.

scare off.meaning: To make a person or animal go away by frightening them.
scare off.example: He had scared off a leopard!

sign language.meaning: A language that uses hand movements instead of spoken words. People who cannot hear use it.
sign language.example: A captive gorilla named Koko has even learned sign language.

sit up.meaning: To move from lying down to sitting.

spit out.meaning: To push something out of your mouth.

stick out.meaning: To push something out, or to come out from a place. "Stick out your tongue" means push your tongue out of your mouth, often to be funny.
stick out.example: she stuck out her tongue at us!

stick to.meaning: To stay on something as if it were glued.
stick to.example: His wet clothes stuck to his skin.

stop in one's tracks.meaning: To stop suddenly, because you are surprised or afraid.

take a deep breath.meaning: To breathe in a lot of air, often to make yourself calm.

take notes.meaning: To write down things that you see or hear, so you can remember them.
take notes.example: He’s never seen anyone take notes before.

take off.meaning: 1. To leave or run away quickly. 2. To take clothes or a bag off your body.
take off.example: She took off down the ladder.

take off after.meaning: To start to run after someone quickly.
take off after.example: She took off after the small gorilla.

tear to pieces.meaning: To pull something apart into many pieces.
tear to pieces.example: find him and tear him to pieces.

that does it.meaning: "That finishes it; we have done what we needed to do."
that does it.example: “Well,” Annie said with a sigh, “I guess that does it.”

the rest.meaning: The other part that is left.

throw oneself.meaning: To jump or fall down suddenly and hard.
throw oneself.example: Then he threw himself on his belly.

time and space.example: She travels through time and space, gathering books.

too late.meaning: After the time when something could be done.

turn into.meaning: 1. To change and become something different. 2. "Turn to someone" = turn your body so that you face them.
turn into.example: The fog had turned into a fine mist.

up to.meaning: 1. As much as; not more than. 2. "Go back up to" a place = go up to it again.
up to.example: A silverback gorilla can eat up to 50 pounds of forest vegetation in only one day.

vampire bat.meaning: A small bat from Central and South America that drinks the blood of animals.

what's wrong.example: “What’s wrong?” said Jack, standing beneath the trees.

worst of all.meaning: The most bad thing of all.
worst of all.example: Worst of all, he couldn’t find Annie.

you know.meaning: 1. Words that people add when they talk, to make sure the other person is listening. 2. "Didn't you know?" = did you not know that?
you know.example: There are different kinds of rain forests, you know.

oh man.meaning: Something you say when you feel strongly: surprised, afraid, tired or happy. "Oh, man!" is like "Oh, wow!" or "Oh, no!" It is not about a real man.
